descripcion: At C1 the focus shifts to verbs where gerund and infinitive both exist but shift the meaning subtly — regret, go on, mean — and to distinguishing perfect gerunds (having done) from simple ones, which mark that an action happened before the main verb.

cuadroReferencia.notaPie: Having done + past participle marks that the gerund's action happened before the main verb: having finished the report, she left.

ejemplos.texto: I regret to say the meeting has been cancelled.
He went on to explain the reasoning behind the decision.
Having finished early, she decided to review it again.

notas: Regret + infinitive is used almost exclusively for formal announcements of bad news; regret + gerund is a genuine personal regret.
Go on + gerund means to continue doing the same thing; go on + infinitive means to move on to something new.
A perfect gerund (having + participle) is a compact way to show that one action clearly preceded another.

es.en: Spanish uses the infinitive more generally and does not mark these meaning differences as systematically. Spanish speakers tend to learn these verbs as isolated exceptions, without seeing the pattern that the gerund points to continuity or an earlier action and the infinitive to a next or different step.
es.es: El español usa el infinitivo de forma más general y no marca estas diferencias de significado de manera tan sistemática. Los hispanohablantes tienden a aprender estos verbos como excepciones aisladas, sin ver el patrón: el gerundio suele apuntar a continuidad o a una acción anterior, y el infinitivo a un paso siguiente o distinto.

de.en: German has no gerund, only the zu-infinitive, and marks these meaning differences with different constructions (vergessen, etwas zu tun gegen vergessen, dass man etwas getan hat). German speakers therefore default to the to-infinitive, and the perfect gerund is often calqued from the German perfect infinitive: I regret to have said instead of I regret having said.
de.de: Deutsch hat kein Gerundium, sondern den «zu»-Infinitiv und markiert Bedeutungsunterschiede mit verschiedenen Konstruktionen («vergessen, etwas zu tun» gegenüber «vergessen, dass man etwas getan hat»). Deutschsprachige greifen daher zum to-infinitive; das perfect gerund wird oft aus dem deutschen Perfektinfinitiv wörtlich übertragen: «I regret to have said» statt «I regret having said».

it.en: Italian marks several of these distinctions with other means: smettere di fare (stop doing) against fermarsi a fare (stop to do), ricordarsi di fare against ricordarsi di aver fatto. The second pair leads to the calque I remember to have done instead of I remember doing, so the perfect gerund needs special attention.
it.it: L'italiano marca varie di queste differenze con altri mezzi: «smettere di fare» («stop doing») contro «fermarsi a fare» («stop to do»), «ricordarsi di fare» contro «ricordarsi di aver fatto». La seconda coppia porta al calco «I remember to have done» invece di «I remember doing», quindi il perfect gerund richiede attenzione speciale.

fr.en: French marks the difference between remembering an earlier action and a later duty with the perfect infinitive (se souvenir d'avoir fait). Translated literally, regretter d'avoir dit becomes I regret to have said instead of I regret having said, so the perfect gerund is the main point for French speakers.
fr.fr: Le français marque la différence entre le souvenir d'une action antérieure et une obligation ultérieure grâce à l'infinitif passé («se souvenir d'avoir fait»). Traduit littéralement, «regretter d'avoir dit» devient «I regret to have said» au lieu de «I regret having said» ; le perfect gerund est donc le point principal.

pt.en: Portuguese marks several of these distinctions lexically: continuar a fazer (go on doing) against passar a fazer (go on to do). The perfect infinitive (lembro-me de ter feito) leads to the calque I remember to have done instead of I remember doing.
pt.pt: O português marca várias dessas diferenças lexicalmente: «continuar a fazer» («go on doing») contra «passar a fazer» («go on to do»). O infinitivo perfeito («lembro-me de ter feito») pode levar ao calque «I remember to have done» em vez de «I remember doing».

errores: Using regret + infinitive for a genuine personal regret instead of a formal announcement.
Confusing went on doing and went on to do.
Using a simple gerund where a perfect gerund would clarify the sequence of events.

traducciones.de: Ich bedaure sagen zu müssen, dass…

redemittel.funcion: repairs the wrong choice out loud

autochequeo: Is regret used correctly for formal announcement versus personal regret?
Is went on followed by the right form for continuation versus a new step?
Is a perfect gerund used where the sequence of events needs clarifying?
Do the subtle meaning shifts match what I actually intend to say?
Are at least five of these nuanced verbs used correctly?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on gerunds and infinitives with a meaning shift: regret, go on, mean, and perfect gerunds. Check whether the chosen form matches the intended meaning. Do not rewrite the text.

es: «*acordarse de haber hecho*» rendered as *remember to have done* instead of *remember doing*.
de: *es gewohnt sein, … zu* rendered with an infinitive: *I am used to work late* instead of *I am used to working late*.
it: «*ricordarsi di aver fatto*» rendered as *remember to have done* instead of *remember doing*.
fr: «*avoir l'habitude de*» rendered with an infinitive: *I am used to work late* instead of *I am used to working late*.
pt: «*lembrar-se de ter feito*» rendered as *remember to have done* instead of *remember doing*.
